```{r setup}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(knitr)

# Render from the project root so these relative paths work
samples   <- read_csv("data/processed/samples.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
genus     <- read_csv("data/processed/community_genus_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
family    <- read_csv("data/processed/community_family_long.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
clean_log <- read_csv("outputs/tables/data_cleaning_log.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

within   <- read_csv("outputs/tables/permanova_within_station.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
between  <- read_csv("outputs/tables/permanova_impact_between.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
bdisp    <- read_csv("outputs/tables/betadisper.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nmds_sum <- read_csv("outputs/tables/nmds_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
change   <- read_csv("outputs/tables/station_change.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pca_var  <- read_csv("outputs/tables/env_pca_variance.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
simper   <- read_csv("outputs/tables/simper_hi_vs_ni.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sfc      <- read_csv("outputs/tables/simper_family_cp.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cp1g     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/cp1_genera_at_hi.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
est      <- read_csv("outputs/tables/colonizer_model_estimates.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
mfit     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/colonizer_model_fit.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
sens     <- read_csv("outputs/tables/colonizer_model_sensitivity.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
fitted   <- read_csv("outputs/tables/colonizer_model_fitted.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
e_       <- function(prefix) est[startsWith(est$parameter, prefix), ]
cp_means <- read_csv("outputs/tables/cp_composition_stations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  summarise(m = mean(pct), .by = c(year, impact, cp))
cpv <- function(y, g, k) cp_means$m[cp_means$year == y & cp_means$impact == g & cp_means$cp == k]
bg       <- read_csv("outputs/tables/control_background.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
dmodel   <- read_csv("outputs/tables/distance_model_effects.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

pick     <- function(df, tr, trm) df |> filter(transform == tr, term == trm)
pick_eff <- function(tr, resp, eff) dmodel |> filter(transform == tr, response == resp, effect == eff)

yr  <- pick(within, "sqrt", "year_f")
ixn <- pick(within, "sqrt", "impact:year_f")
imp <- pick(between, "sqrt", "Model")
chg <- change |> filter(transform == "sqrt")

pool_sqrt <- pick_eff("sqrt", "gap", "Change per year, HI and MI pooled")
pool_raw  <- pick_eff("raw", "gap", "Change per year, HI and MI pooled")
bg_sqrt   <- bg |> filter(transform == "sqrt")

fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
```

## Background and question

The 2010 Deepwater Horizon blowout released a very large amount of oil into the Gulf of Mexico, and some of it reached the deep seafloor. Nematodes dominate the small animal communities in deep sea sediment. They spend their whole lives in the mud and reproduce quickly, and earlier work suggests they can recover faster than many other sediment animals after a disturbance (Brannock et al. 2017). That makes them a reasonable group in which to look for early signs of recovery, although it is an expectation we would like to examine with data.

Our main question is whether, between 2010 and 2011, the nematode communities at oil impacted stations became more similar to those at unimpacted stations. Our working hypothesis is that they did. If recovery was under way, we would expect the heavily and moderately impacted stations to move toward the unimpacted ones, and eventually to differ from them no more than the unimpacted stations differ from each other. This last point matters because two healthy sites are never identical, so we take "recovered" to mean "within the normal range of variation among controls" and not "identical to a control."

We originally planned a simulation model that projected recovery forward to 2022. With only two sampling years there is too little information to say how recovery proceeds over a decade, so after discussing it with our instructor we chose a simpler design. We describe how the communities compare, ask whether the differences are larger than we would expect by chance, and measure directly whether impacted stations moved closer to the controls. The analysis can be rerun from the scripts in the `scripts` folder, and the numbers quoted below are read from the files those scripts produce.

## The data

Samples come from nine stations: three heavily impacted (HI), three moderately impacted (MI), and three not impacted (NI), which serve as controls. Each station was sampled in 2010 and 2011, and at each visit the sediment was divided into a surface layer (0 to 1 cm) and a deeper layer (1 to 3 cm), giving `r nrow(samples)` samples in total. Nematodes were counted and identified to genus where possible, and always to family. The workbook also contains summary indices and environmental measurements, but here we use only community composition, since the indices are calculated from that same composition.

The two layers at a station come from the same location and are not independent, so we averaged them. Each station in each year is therefore one observation, which leaves 18 observations from nine stations. Two features of the data shaped how we worked. First, the 2010 values are percentages while the 2011 values are counts of roughly 100 animals per sample, so we converted everything to percent. This lets us compare what the communities are made of, but not how many animals are present. Second, the genus lists differ between years (`r n_distinct(genus$genus[genus$year == 2010], na.rm = TRUE)` genera in 2010 and `r n_distinct(genus$genus[genus$year == 2011], na.rm = TRUE)` in 2011). Some of this is probably real, and some reflects spelling and how finely animals were identified. To avoid reading naming differences as ecological change, we compared the years at the family level (`r n_distinct(family$family)` families). Every cleaning decision is recorded in the appendix.

In symbols, let $c_{sik}$ be the count (or, for 2010, the percentage) of family $k$ in layer $i$ at station-year $s$. We first convert it to a percentage of that layer's total, then average the two layers:

$$
p_{sik} = 100 \, \frac{c_{sik}}{\sum_k c_{sik}}, \qquad x_{sk} = \frac{p_{s1k} + p_{s2k}}{2}.
$$

Most analyses use the square root of this value, $y_{sk} = \sqrt{x_{sk}}$, and we repeated them with $x_{sk}$ itself as a check.

## Comparing communities

To compare two communities we need a number that says how different they are. We used the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, which compares the percentage of each family in two samples:

$$
BC_{ij} = \frac{\sum_k |y_{ik} - y_{jk}|}{\sum_k (y_{ik} + y_{jk})}
$$

where $y_{ik}$ is the transformed percentage of family $k$ in station-year $i$. It ranges from 0 (the same mix of families) to 1 (no families in common). We applied it to square root transformed percentages so that a few very common families do not dominate the result, and repeated every analysis on untransformed percentages as a check.

To see the overall pattern we used non metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS). This takes all of the pairwise dissimilarities and draws a two dimensional map in which similar communities sit close together. Squeezing the information into two dimensions loses some detail, which is summarized by the stress value (`r sprintf("%.2f", nmds_sum$stress[nmds_sum$transform == "sqrt"])` here). That is acceptable for reading the general layout but not for interpreting small differences between neighbouring points. The axes have no units, and only the distances between points are meaningful.

Formally, NMDS places the station-years on the map so that distances between points keep the same rank order as the dissimilarities, and the stress measures how well it manages (Kruskal 1964):

$$
\text{Stress} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i<j} (d_{ij} - \hat{d}_{ij})^2}{\sum_{i<j} d_{ij}^2}},
$$

where $d_{ij}$ is the distance between station-years $i$ and $j$ on the map and $\hat{d}_{ij}$ is the target distance obtained by fitting a monotone function of $BC_{ij}$. Lower values mean the map reproduces the dissimilarities more closely.

```{r nmds-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Community similarity at the family level. Arrows connect each station's 2010 position (circle) to its 2011 position (triangle). Stations that are close together have similar communities."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/nmds_trajectories.png")
```

Two patterns appear in the map. The stations are ordered by impact level along the horizontal axis, with heavily impacted stations on the left, unimpacted stations on the right, and moderately impacted stations in between, in both years. Almost every station also moved in the same direction between years, including the unimpacted controls, and by a similar amount (`r sprintf("%.2f", min(chg$bc_2010_to_2011))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(chg$bc_2010_to_2011))` in Bray-Curtis units). The impacted stations therefore did not visibly move toward the controls. They shifted along with everything else.

## Testing whether the patterns are likely to be real

With nine stations it is easy to see structure that is not there, so we tested the patterns with PERMANOVA. The test first measures how strongly the groups of interest (impact level or year) separate the communities. It then shuffles the group labels many times and measures the separation each time. If the real labels separate the communities better than nearly all of the shuffled versions, the pattern is unlikely to be chance, and the proportion of shuffles that do as well gives the p value. The R squared value tells us how much of the total difference between communities the grouping accounts for.

The formulas (Anderson 2001) work directly from the dissimilarities among the $N$ station-years. For a single grouping with $a$ groups, where group $g$ has $n_g$ members,

$$
SS_T = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i<j} BC_{ij}^2, \qquad SS_W = \sum_{g=1}^{a} \frac{1}{n_g} \sum_{i<j \in g} BC_{ij}^2, \qquad SS_A = SS_T - SS_W,
$$

and the test statistic and effect size are

$$
F = \frac{SS_A / (a - 1)}{SS_W / (N - a)}, \qquad R^2 = \frac{SS_A}{SS_T}.
$$

The p value is the proportion of label shuffles that give an $F$ at least as large as the one from the real labels. With impact, year and their interaction in the model, the same calculation is applied to each term in turn.

Impact level belongs to a station and does not change, whereas year varies within a station, so the two effects needed different shuffling. For year, and for whether the change over the year differed by impact level, we shuffled year labels within each station. With two years per station there are only 512 possible arrangements, so the smallest attainable p value is about 0.004. For impact level we averaged each station's two years and shuffled whole stations among groups.

```{r permanova-table}
bind_rows(
  yr  |> mutate(Test = "Year"),
  ixn |> mutate(Test = "Impact x year"),
  imp |> mutate(Test = "Impact level")
) |>
  transmute(Test, `R squared` = R2, F = F, p = fmt_p(`Pr(>F)`)) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "PERMANOVA results (square root data). Year and impact x year use shuffling within stations, and impact level uses shuffling of whole stations.")
```

Impact level explained a large share of the differences among stations (R squared `r sprintf("%.2f", imp$R2)`, p = `r fmt_p(imp$"Pr(>F)")`), and year explained a smaller but detectable share (`r sprintf("%.2f", yr$R2)`, p = `r fmt_p(yr$"Pr(>F)")`). The interaction between impact and year is the term most relevant to recovery, because it asks whether the change over the year differed among impact levels. We did not detect such a difference (R squared `r sprintf("%.2f", ixn$R2)`, p = `r fmt_p(ixn$"Pr(>F)")`). A check on the method's assumption that groups are similarly spread out raised no concerns (p = `r fmt_p(bdisp$p[bdisp$transform == "sqrt"])`), although with three stations per group it could only detect large departures. Untransformed data gave the same overall pattern.

## Distance to the controls

The analyses above describe all communities together. To address our question more directly, we calculated for each HI and MI station and year the average Bray-Curtis dissimilarity to the three NI stations sampled that year. If a station were recovering, this distance should shrink over time. For station $s$ in year $t$,

$$
D_{st} = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{c \in \text{NI}} BC\big((s,t),(c,t)\big),
$$

where the sum runs over the three unimpacted stations $c$ sampled in the same year.

We also needed a sense of how different healthy sites normally are. For each year we averaged the dissimilarity across the three possible pairs of NI stations, which we call the background. It was `r sprintf("%.2f", bg_sqrt$background[bg_sqrt$year == 2010])` in 2010 and `r sprintf("%.2f", bg_sqrt$background[bg_sqrt$year == 2011])` in 2011. A recovered station would have a distance close to this background, not close to zero. The gap is a station's distance minus the background for the same year. Writing these out,

$$
B_t = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{c < c'} BC\big((c,t),(c',t)\big), \qquad G_{st} = D_{st} - B_t,
$$

where the sum for $B_t$ runs over the three pairs of unimpacted stations.

```{r distance-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Average dissimilarity between each impacted station and the unimpacted stations. The dashed line is the background, the average dissimilarity among unimpacted stations."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/distance_to_control.png")
```

Heavily impacted stations were furthest from the controls in both years, and most lines tilt upward, not downward. To quantify this we used a mixed model, a regression in which each station has its own baseline so that stations that are simply further from the controls do not get mistaken for an effect of time. It estimates the change per year in the gap, where a negative value would indicate movement toward the controls. The model is

$$
G_{st} = \beta_{g(s)} + \gamma_{g(s)} (t - 2010) + u_s + \varepsilon_{st}, \qquad u_s \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2), \quad \varepsilon_{st} \sim N(0, \sigma^2),
$$

where $g(s)$ is the impact level of station $s$ (HI or MI), $\beta_g$ is the average gap for that level in 2010, $\gamma_g$ is the change in gap per year, $u_s$ is the station's own offset, and $\varepsilon_{st}$ is the remaining variation. The pooled version uses a single $\gamma$ shared by HI and MI. We fitted the models by restricted maximum likelihood with the `nlme` package (Pinheiro and Bates 2000), and the intervals in the table are 95% confidence intervals for $\gamma$. The same model was also fitted with the distance $D_{st}$ in place of the gap.

```{r distance-model}
dmodel |>
  filter(response == "gap", !grepl("^Difference", effect)) |>
  transmute(
    Data = recode(transform, sqrt = "Square root", raw = "Untransformed"),
    Group = sub("Change per year, ", "", effect),
    `Change per year` = estimate,
    `95% interval` = sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", lower, upper),
    p = fmt_p(p)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(Data)) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Estimated change per year in the gap between impacted stations and the controls. Twelve observations from six stations.")
```

No estimate pointed toward recovery. With square root data the gap increased by about `r sprintf("%.3f", pool_sqrt$estimate)` per year for HI and MI combined (95% interval `r sprintf("%.3f", pool_sqrt$lower)` to `r sprintf("%.3f", pool_sqrt$upper)`), but with untransformed data the estimate was smaller (`r sprintf("%.3f", pool_raw$estimate)`) and its interval included zero (`r sprintf("%.3f", pool_raw$lower)` to `r sprintf("%.3f", pool_raw$upper)`). Because the result depends on the transformation, we interpret it cautiously. We found no evidence that impacted stations moved closer to the controls, and we do not think the data support a firm claim that they moved away.

## Other views of the data

A few supporting figures help show what sits behind the main results. They are descriptive, and with three stations per impact level we do not draw firm conclusions from them.

We first asked whether the environmental measurements tell the same story as the communities. A principal component analysis (PCA) condenses several correlated measurements, here depth, aluminium, barium, PAH44, total petroleum hydrocarbons, mud content, and organic carbon, into a few new axes that capture as much of the variation among stations as possible. Stations that sit close together on the plot have similar environmental profiles, and an arrow shows which measurements push stations in which direction. We ran it separately for each year because the 2010 and 2011 values look to be on different scales, so the two panels should not be compared axis for axis.

Each variable $v$ is log transformed where noted and then standardized, $z_{sv} = (w_{sv} - \bar{w}_v) / \text{sd}(w_v)$, so that all variables count equally. The axes come from the eigendecomposition of the correlation matrix,

$$
\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{V} \mathbf{\Lambda} \mathbf{V}^\top,
$$

the position of station $s$ on axis $m$ is $\sum_v z_{sv} V_{vm}$, and the share of the variation captured by axis $m$ is $\lambda_m / \sum_m \lambda_m$.

```{r pca-fig}
#| fig-cap: "PCA of environmental variables, run separately for each year. Arrows show how each variable relates to the two axes, and the percentages show how much of the variation each axis captures."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/env_pca.png")
```

In both years the first axis explains most of the variation (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pca_var$prop_variance[pca_var$year == 2010 & pca_var$PC == "PC1"])`% in 2010 and `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pca_var$prop_variance[pca_var$year == 2011 & pca_var$PC == "PC1"])`% in 2011), and barium, PAH44, and total petroleum hydrocarbons point in the same direction along it. The heavily impacted stations sit at the hydrocarbon end in both years, while the moderately impacted and unimpacted stations overlap on the other side. In environmental terms, then, the heavily impacted stations stand apart from the rest, but the moderately impacted stations look much like the controls, even though their communities fall between the two groups on the NMDS map. Organic carbon also behaves differently between years, lining up with the hydrocarbons in 2011 but not in 2010, which is another reason to check how the environmental data were measured.

```{r comp-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Percent composition of the ten most abundant nematode families at each station, averaged over the two sediment layers. All remaining families are grouped as Other."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/family_composition.png")
```

The composition bars show what the NMDS map is summarizing. Xyalidae and Monhysteridae make up much of every station, but Monhysteridae takes up a larger share at the heavily impacted stations in both years, while Chromadoridae and Comesomatidae are more prominent at the unimpacted ones. The next section looks more closely at which families drive the difference between impact levels.

```{r idx-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Maturity index (MI) and index of trophic diversity (ITD) for each station in 2010 and 2011, averaged over the two layers. MI values are recalculated from the cleaned data because the 2010 workbook values appear to contain an error."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/indices_mi_itd.png")
```

The two summary indices are shown for readers who know them from the literature. Low maturity index values indicate communities dominated by opportunistic nematodes, and ITD summarizes how evenly the four feeding types are represented, with values near 0.25 meaning all four are equally common and values near 1 meaning one type dominates. If $f_{si}$ is the proportion of genus $i$ at station-year $s$, $v_i$ is its c-p value (explained below), and $\theta_{sj}$ is the proportion of the community in feeding group $j$, then

$$
MI_s = \sum_i v_i f_{si}, \qquad ITD_s = \sum_{j=1}^{4} \theta_{sj}^2
$$

(Bongers 1990; Heip et al. 1985). From 2010 to 2011 the maturity index rose and ITD fell at most moderately impacted and unimpacted stations, while the heavily impacted stations changed in mixed directions. This is the same general picture as before, with most stations shifting together between years and no clear sign that the heavily impacted stations were catching up.

```{r map-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Station locations (2010 coordinates). No coastline is drawn because the stations all lie within a few kilometres of each other."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/site_map.png")
```

The site map shows that the three heavily impacted stations are clustered in the north, the unimpacted stations lie mostly to the south and east, and the moderately impacted stations are scattered toward the edges. Because impact level and location are partly tangled together, differences between impact groups could also reflect other features that vary across the area, such as depth or sediment type, and we cannot fully separate those with this design.

## Which families differ most between heavily impacted and unimpacted stations

The composition bars suggest that some families change with impact level, so we asked which ones account for most of the difference. We used a method called SIMPER. It starts from the average Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between the heavily impacted and unimpacted stations (`r sprintf("%.2f", sum(simper$contribution))` here) and splits it into a contribution from each family. A family contributes a lot when its abundance differs between the two groups and does so consistently across stations. This is a descriptive tool. We did not attach p values, because the two years at a station are not independent and there are only three stations per group. As a check, we also ranked the families separately within each year, using three heavily impacted and three unimpacted stations each time.

For a pair of station-years $i$ (HI) and $j$ (NI), family $k$ contributes (Clarke 1993)

$$
\delta_{ij,k} = \frac{|y_{ik} - y_{jk}|}{\sum_k (y_{ik} + y_{jk})}, \qquad \sum_k \delta_{ij,k} = BC_{ij}.
$$

SIMPER averages this over all HI and NI pairs, $\bar{\delta}_k = \text{mean}_{i,j} \, \delta_{ij,k}$, and ranks the families by $\bar{\delta}_k$. The share of the difference in the table below is $\bar{\delta}_k / \sum_k \bar{\delta}_k$.

```{r simper-fig}
#| fig-cap: "The eight families contributing most to the difference between heavily impacted (HI) and unimpacted (NI) communities. Colour shows which group had the higher average abundance."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/simper_hi_vs_ni.png")
```

```{r simper-table}
simper |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  transmute(
    Rank = rank,
    Family = family,
    `Share of difference (%)` = 100 * (cumulative - lag(cumulative, default = 0)),
    `Mean % at HI` = mean_pct_HI,
    `Mean % at NI` = mean_pct_NI,
    `Rank in 2010` = rank_2010,
    `Rank in 2011` = rank_2011
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 1, caption = "Families contributing most to the HI versus NI difference (square root data for ranking, untransformed percent for the means).")
```

One family stands out. Monhysteridae accounts for about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * simper$cumulative[1])`% of the difference, averaging `r sprintf("%.0f", simper$mean_pct_HI[1])`% of the community at heavily impacted stations compared with `r sprintf("%.0f", simper$mean_pct_NI[1])`% at unimpacted ones, and it ranked first in both years. Linhomoeidae is also more abundant at the heavily impacted stations, while Chromadoridae, Cyatholaimidae, and Comesomatidae are more abundant at the unimpacted ones. Beyond Monhysteridae the contributions are fairly evenly spread, so the difference between the two groups reflects a number of families shifting a little each, not one or two. The rankings were not equally stable across years. Xyalidae ranked second in 2010 but much lower in 2011, so we would treat the order of the lower ranked families as uncertain.

Our proposal drew on the idea that opportunistic nematodes tend to increase after a disturbance while sensitive ones decline (Ridall and Ingels 2021), so we checked whether these families fit that idea. Each genus in the dataset has a colonizer and persister (c-p) value from 1 to 5. Low values describe fast reproducing, tolerant animals that tend to do well in disturbed sediment, and high values describe slow reproducing, sensitive animals. If the heavily impacted stations were dominated by opportunists, they should have more of their communities in the lowest classes. Using the same notation as above, the share of a station-year's community in c-p class $c$ is

$$
P_{sc} = 100 \sum_{i:\, v_i = c} f_{si},
$$

and the c-p value we quote for a family $k$ is the abundance weighted average over its genera,

$$
\bar{v}_k = \frac{\sum_{i \in k} v_i a_i}{\sum_{i \in k} a_i},
$$

where $a_i$ is the total abundance of genus $i$ across all samples.

```{r cp-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Share of each community in each c-p class (1 = colonizers, 5 = persisters) for heavily impacted (HI) and unimpacted (NI) stations. Bars are group means and points are individual stations."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/cp_composition.png")
```

The pattern does fit. Animals with a c-p value of 1 made up about `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2010, "HI", 1))`% of heavily impacted communities in 2010 and `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2011, "HI", 1))`% in 2011, compared with `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2010, "NI", 1))`% and `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2011, "NI", 1))`% at unimpacted stations, and in both years every heavily impacted station had more of them than every unimpacted one. Nearly all of this (about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * cp1g$share_of_cp1_at_HI[1])`%) comes from a single genus, `r cp1g$genus[1]`, in the Monhysteridae, which matches Monhysteridae being the family that separates the groups most (its abundance weighted c-p value is `r sprintf("%.1f", sfc$mean_cp[sfc$family == "Monhysteridae"])`). Unimpacted stations, in turn, had more of their communities in classes 2 and 3. The two families with the highest c-p values among our top eight, Desmoscolecidae and Oxystominidae (about `r sprintf("%.1f", sfc$mean_cp[sfc$family == "Desmoscolecidae"])` and `r sprintf("%.1f", sfc$mean_cp[sfc$family == "Oxystominidae"])`), were both more abundant at unimpacted stations, as were Chromadoridae and Cyatholaimidae. The fit is not perfect, however. Xyalidae and Comesomatidae, which were also more abundant at unimpacted stations, have low values (about `r sprintf("%.1f", sfc$mean_cp[sfc$family == "Xyalidae"])` and `r sprintf("%.1f", sfc$mean_cp[sfc$family == "Comesomatidae"])`), and Linhomoeidae, more abundant at heavily impacted stations, has a middle value (`r sprintf("%.1f", sfc$mean_cp[sfc$family == "Linhomoeidae"])`). The contrast therefore rests mostly on one extreme colonizer genus, and it is not a simple gradient across all families.

This also bears on our main question. Between 2010 and 2011 the share of c-p 1 animals at unimpacted stations fell from about `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2010, "NI", 1))`% to `r sprintf("%.0f", cpv(2011, "NI", 1))`%, while at heavily impacted stations it stayed near 40%. That is the opposite of what we would expect if the heavily impacted communities were becoming more like the controls, and it agrees with the distance to control results, where the gap did not shrink. With three stations per group and no formal test, we treat this as a description and not a conclusion.

## A model for the colonizer share

So far the colonizer result is a description. We also wanted a model that we write down and fit ourselves, so that the size of the effect and its uncertainty come from a likelihood we can inspect. The colonizer share is a good target because it is the clearest difference between the groups, and because it is naturally a count out of a total: of all the nematodes identified at a station in a year, how many have a c-p value of 1?

For 2011 these counts are in the dataset. For 2010 we only have percentages, so we reconstructed each sample's size by finding the number of animals that turns its percentages into whole numbers (falling back on assuming the rarest taxon was a single animal). The reconstructed sizes are mostly between 90 and 130 animals per layer, although a few samples are much smaller (as few as 45), and the reconstruction is an approximation. To check how much it matters, we refitted the model with every 2010 sample size halved and then doubled.

Let $y_{st}$ be the number of c-p 1 animals at station $s$ in year $t$ (summed over the two layers) out of $n_{st}$ animals in total. A plain binomial model would treat every animal as an independent draw with the same chance $p$ of being a colonizer, but stations of the same impact level clearly differ from one another by more than that. We therefore let each station's true proportion vary around $p_{st}$, which gives the beta binomial distribution:

$$
y_{st} \sim \text{BetaBinomial}(n_{st}, p_{st}, \kappa), \qquad
P(y \mid n, p, \kappa) = \binom{n}{y} \frac{B\big(y + p\kappa,\; n - y + (1-p)\kappa\big)}{B\big(p\kappa,\; (1-p)\kappa\big)},
$$

where $B$ is the beta function. The parameter $\kappa$ controls the extra variation between stations, with small values meaning more variation and very large values reducing the model to the binomial. The mean proportion depends on impact level and year through a logistic regression:

$$
\text{logit}(p_{st}) = a + b_{HI} \, HI_s + b_{MI} \, MI_s + \big(c + d_{HI} \, HI_s + d_{MI} \, MI_s\big)(t - 2010),
$$

where $HI_s$ and $MI_s$ are indicators for the impact level of station $s$. Here $a$ is the log odds of colonizers at unimpacted stations in 2010, $b_{HI}$ and $b_{MI}$ are how much higher (or lower) the log odds are at HI and MI stations in 2010, $c$ is the yearly change in log odds at unimpacted stations, and $d_{HI}$ and $d_{MI}$ are how much the yearly change at HI and MI stations differs from that at unimpacted stations. The parameter that speaks most directly to our question is $d_{HI}$. If heavily impacted stations were converging on the controls, their colonizer share would fall relative to the controls and $d_{HI}$ would be negative.

We estimated the seven parameters by maximum likelihood. Writing $\theta$ for all of them, we minimized the negative log likelihood

$$
-\ell(\theta) = -\sum_{s,t} \log P\big(y_{st} \mid n_{st}, p_{st}(\theta), \kappa\big)
$$

with `optim` (the BFGS method), using the same approach as in lab. For the uncertainty we used profile likelihood intervals. For a parameter $\theta_j$, the profile likelihood fixes $\theta_j$ at a trial value, re-maximizes the likelihood over all the other parameters, and records the result:

$$
\ell_p(\theta_j) = \max_{\theta_{-j}} \ell(\theta_j, \theta_{-j}).
$$

The 95% interval contains every value of $\theta_j$ for which $2\big[\ell(\hat\theta) - \ell_p(\theta_j)\big] \le \chi^2_{1,\,0.95}$, which means the negative log likelihood is no more than about 1.92 above its minimum. Unlike a Wald interval ($\hat\theta \pm 1.96 \, \text{SE}$), this does not assume the likelihood is symmetric, which matters with so few stations. We report log odds and odds ratios $\exp(\theta)$.

```{r colonizer-fit-table}
mfit |>
  transmute(Model = model, Parameters = n_parameters, `Negative log likelihood` = neg_log_lik, AIC) |>
  kable(digits = 1, caption = "Comparison of the beta binomial and plain binomial models. Lower AIC is better.")
```

The beta binomial model is much better supported than the plain binomial (AIC of `r sprintf("%.0f", mfit$AIC[mfit$model == "Beta-binomial"])` against `r sprintf("%.0f", mfit$AIC[mfit$model == "Binomial"])`), so stations of the same impact level do differ by more than counting error would produce. The estimated $\kappa$ is about `r sprintf("%.0f", sens$kappa[sens$scale_2010_n == 1])`.

```{r colonizer-est-table}
est |>
  transmute(
    Parameter = parameter,
    Estimate = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
    `95% profile interval` = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", profile_lower, profile_upper),
    `Odds ratio` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", odds_ratio, or_lower, or_upper)
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Maximum likelihood estimates on the log odds scale, with profile likelihood intervals and odds ratios.")
```

```{r colonizer-profile-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Profile likelihoods for the 2010 difference between HI and NI stations (left) and for the difference in yearly change (right). The 95% interval is where the curve lies below the dashed line."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/colonizer_profiles.png")
```

```{r colonizer-fit-fig}
#| fig-cap: "Observed colonizer proportions at each station and the fitted group means from the beta binomial model."
include_graphics("outputs/figures/colonizer_fit.png")
```

In 2010 the odds of a colonizer animal were about `r sprintf("%.1f", e_("bHI")$odds_ratio)` times higher at heavily impacted stations than at unimpacted ones (95% profile interval `r sprintf("%.1f", e_("bHI")$or_lower)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", e_("bHI")$or_upper)`). At unimpacted stations the odds fell sharply over the year, to about `r sprintf("%.2f", e_("c (")$odds_ratio)` of their earlier value (interval `r sprintf("%.2f", e_("c (")$or_lower)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", e_("c (")$or_upper)`), which is a drop in the fitted proportion from about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * fitted$p[fitted$impact == "NI" & fitted$year == 2010])`% to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * fitted$p[fitted$impact == "NI" & fitted$year == 2011])`%. At heavily impacted stations the fitted proportion barely moved (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * fitted$p[fitted$impact == "HI" & fitted$year == 2010])`% to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * fitted$p[fitted$impact == "HI" & fitted$year == 2011])`%). The difference in yearly change, $d_{HI}$, is therefore positive (`r sprintf("%.2f", e_("dHI")$estimate)`, profile interval `r sprintf("%.2f", e_("dHI")$profile_lower)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", e_("dHI")$profile_upper)`), and its interval excludes zero. The moderately impacted stations sit in between, but their intervals include zero for both the 2010 difference and the change. The results hardly changed when the reconstructed 2010 sample sizes were halved or doubled ($\hat{d}_{HI}$ stayed between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(sens$dHI))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(sens$dHI))`).

The important point is the direction. A positive $d_{HI}$ means the gap between heavily impacted and unimpacted stations in colonizer share widened. It did not widen because the colonizers increased at heavily impacted stations, but because they dropped at the unimpacted ones while staying high at the heavily impacted ones. This is the opposite of convergence, so this model gives no evidence of recovery in the colonizer share by 2011. What it cannot tell us is why the unimpacted stations changed so much. The drop could be a real regional change, but it could equally reflect differences in sampling or identification between the years, and with two years of data we cannot separate the two. The model also rests on 18 observations and seven parameters, treats the animals counted at a station as independent draws given the station's proportion, and uses reconstructed sample sizes for 2010, so the intervals should be read as rough.

## What the results suggest, and their limits

Oil impacted and unimpacted stations hosted different nematode communities in both years. Between 2010 and 2011 the whole study area shifted in a similar way, including the unimpacted stations, and we did not detect that impacted stations changed differently from the rest or that they moved closer to the controls. The clearest difference in composition was a larger share of colonizer animals at the heavily impacted stations, almost all of them the genus Halomonhystera, which is what we would expect if opportunistic nematodes are favored at oil impacted sites, and that share did not decline over the year. A beta binomial model of the colonizer share agrees: the odds of a colonizer animal at heavily impacted stations were about `r sprintf("%.1f", e_("bHI")$odds_ratio)` times those at unimpacted stations in 2010 (95% profile interval `r sprintf("%.1f", e_("bHI")$or_lower)` to `r sprintf("%.1f", e_("bHI")$or_upper)`), and the gap widened over the year. This is consistent with a disturbance effect, but we cannot show that oil caused it, because we have no data from before the spill and impact level is partly tangled with location. These results do not support recovery by 2011, but they also do not show that recovery is absent. A single year is a short time over which to expect it.

The most important limitation is the shift shared by all stations. Because the controls changed as much as the impacted stations, we cannot say whether this reflects a real change across the region or differences between years in how samples were collected, subsampled, or identified. Two years of data cannot separate these explanations. With only three stations per impact level, the tests also have limited power, so a result that is not significant is weak evidence that no difference exists. The permutation tests are coarse, working at the family level hides changes within families, and the distance results rest on twelve observations without adjustment for the number of models fitted, so no single p value there should carry much weight.

## Questions about the dataset and next steps

Several questions about the dataset affect how far we can interpret these results. We do not yet know whether sampling, subsampling, and identification methods were the same in both years, or what units the hydrocarbon and metal measurements use in each year, since the values differ greatly between years. The maturity index row for 2010 repeats one value across many samples and may be a copy error. We also do not know whether later surveys, such as a 2023 sampling, exist and are comparable to these.

The last question matters most. Recovery is slow, and later data would let us look at a time span long enough to be informative. It would also allow the analyses our instructor suggested: estimating a recovery rate directly, and testing how well the first two years predict later observations. In the meantime, a useful next step is to compare the families and genera that differ most between heavily impacted and unimpacted stations, particularly Halomonhystera, with published information on how nematodes respond to oil. We chose not to predict the trophic diversity index from genus composition, since the index is calculated from those same genera and the result would be circular.
